newsitem.title: CHINA: China forex reserves seen helping guard HK dollar.
newsitem.headline: China forex reserves seen helping guard HK dollar.

text.p: China, which has the world's second-largest foreign exchange reserves, could build on its treasure chest to guard against attacks on the Hong Kong dollar as other regional currencies face upheaval, analysts said on Tuesday.

"Recently in Southeast Asia there has been a currency crisis, so I think the Chinese government wants to maintain their high reserve policy for some time," said Ken Chan, senior economist for Nikko Research Centre in Hong Kong.
Thailand, the Philippines and Indonesia all recently decided to allow their currencies to float more freely on the market after speculative attacks on them.
Hong Kong has in the past used its foreign exchange reserves to beat off speculative attacks on its currency, which is pegged to the U.S. dollar at a rate of HK$7.80.
China's foreign exchange reserves reached $121.2 billion at the end of June compared with $105 billion at the end of 1996, behind only Japan last year, according to Chinese figures.
Reserves could exceed $130 billion in 1997, analysts said.

A burgeoning trade surplus and continued direct foreign investment had seen reserves swell this year, helped by a deliberate government policy to boost foreign exchange ahead of the Hong Kong handover, analysts said.
"Before the Hong Kong handover, China purposely wanted to build up its foreign exchange reserves," Chan said.
Hong Kong became a Special Administrative Region of China on July 1, passing part of the responsibility for maintaining the value of the former British colony's currency to Beijing.
"They want to hold the high foreign exchange position for some time as currency stability (for Hong Kong) is a top concern of the Chinese government," Chan said.
"In the short term, especially before the October party congress, there will be no big change in policy (towards reserves)," said Liao Quan, senior economist for Standard Chartered Bank in Hong Kong.

The Chinese Communist Party is expected to hold a major meeting around October -- the first such gathering since the death in February of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping -- to chart the country's future development. Stability in the leadup to the meeting is seen as a government priority.
High export growth so far this year and other economic fundamentals had also made it easier for China to increase foreign exchange reserves, analysts said.
China said on Monday it chalked up a trade surplus of $17.77 billion in the first half of 1997, compared with $876 million in the same 1996 period, with exports of $80.82 billion.

Beijing's relatively tight monetary policy had continued to create demand for the local currency, reflected in a steady appreciation of the Chinese yuan on the Shanghai-based national foreign exchange market, dealers said.

"International trade and foreign investment are still very healthy so the U.S. dollar supply is still very big," said one dealer, adding the central bank had steadily bought the U.S. currency to keep the yuan from gaining too sharply.

The management and composition of China's foreign exchange reserves is shrouded in mystery, but analysts said the bulk was held in U.S. dollars and managed from a dealing room at the People's Bank of China, the central bank, in Beijing.
China was the bogeyman of the world's foreign exchange markets, whose shadowy presence occasionally moved exchange rates, they said.
However, China held a large proportion of its reserves in U.S. government bonds and other conservative investments, analysts said.
